claims.source: In initial studies, we found that the large Domain 4 was dispensable for skeletogenic function (LvAlx1.ΔD4.GFP) (Figure 5D,D'), while deletion of a region spanning Domains 1–3 abolished rescue (LvAlx1.ΔD123.GFP) (Figure 5E,E').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Deletion of a region spanning Domains 1–3 abolished rescue.
claims.source: In initial studies, we found that the large Domain 4 was dispensable for skeletogenic function (LvAlx1.ΔD4.GFP) (Figure 5D,D'), while deletion of a region spanning Domains 1–3 abolished rescue (LvAlx1.ΔD123.GFP) (Figure 5E,E').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Deletion of Domain 2 alone almost completely abolished rescue.
claims.source: Deletion of Domain 2 alone almost completely abolished rescue (LvAlx1.ΔD2.GFP) (mean percentage of 6a9-positive cells relative to uninjected controls was 7.5%) (Figure 5G,G' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Deletion of Domain 1 did not affect LvAlx1 function.
claims.source: By contrast, deletion of Domain 1 or Domain 3 individually did not affect LvAlx1 function by this assay (LvAlx1.ΔD1.GFP and LvAlx1.ΔD3.GFP) (mean percentages of 6a9-positive cells relative to uninjected controls were 100% and 101%, respectively) (Figure 5F,F',H,H' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Deletion of Domain 3 did not affect LvAlx1 function.
claims.source: By contrast, deletion of Domain 1 or Domain 3 individually did not affect LvAlx1 function by this assay (LvAlx1.ΔD1.GFP and LvAlx1.ΔD3.GFP) (mean percentages of 6a9-positive cells relative to uninjected controls were 100% and 101%, respectively) (Figure 5F,F',H,H' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: A minimal construct containing only the homeodomain and Domains 1 and 2 was sufficient to completely rescue PMC specification and skeletogenesis.
claims.source: We observed that a minimal construct containing only the homeodomain and Domains 1 and 2 was sufficient to completely rescue PMC specification and skeletogenesis (mean percentage of 6a9-positive cells relative to uninjected controls was 98%) (Figure 6F,F' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The minimal functional construct encodes a polypeptide only 132 amino acids in length, less than 1/3 the length of wild-type Alx1 (429 amino acids).
claims.source: This construct encoded a polypeptide only 132 amino acids in length; that is, less than 1/3 the length of wild-type Alx1 (429 amino acids).
claims.evidence: This is a direct calculation based on the construct design.

claims.claim: All mutant Alx1 proteins were expressed at levels very similar to that of LvAlx1.WT.GFP construct.
claims.source: We confirmed by fluorescence microscopy that mutant Alx1 proteins were expressed at levels very similar to that of LvAlx1.WT.GFP construct (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: All mutant Alx1 proteins were localized to the cell nucleus.
claims.source: We also confirmed that all mutant proteins, like wild-type Alx1, were localized to the cell nucleus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy observations.

claims.claim: The homeodomain of LvAlx1 is flanked by NLS motifs that are necessary and sufficient to drive nuclear localization.
claims.source: We analyzed the nuclear localization signals (NLS) of LvAlx1 and found that the homeodomain was flanked by NLS motifs that were necessary and sufficient to drive nuclear localization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Embryos co-injected with LvAlx1 MO and LvAlx1.ΔNΔChargedΔOARΔD34.GFP had normal triradiate spicules at the prism stage and elongated skeletal rods at the pluteus stage.
claims.source: For example, embryos co-injected with LvAlx1 MO and LvAlx1.ΔNΔChargedΔOARΔD34.GFP had normal triradiate spicules at the prism stage and elongated skeletal rods at the pluteus stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,I), confirming that a minimal construct containing just the homeodomain and Domains 1 and 2 was sufficient for complete rescue of LvAlx1 morphants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by DIC microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: LvAlx1 and LvAlx4 share an almost identical homeodomain and a highly conserved OAR domain.
claims.source: The paralogous LvAlx1 and LvAlx4 proteins share an almost identical homeodomain and a highly conserved OAR domain while the remaining protein sequences are mostly dissimilar (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: LvAlx4 lacks Domain 2.
claims.source: In particular, LvAlx4 lacks Domain 2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: LvAlx4.WT.GFP mRNA was unable to replace LvAlx1 in specifying PMCs.
claims.source: We found that LvAlx4.WT.GFP mRNA was unable to replace LvAlx1 in specifying PMCs (mean percentage of 6a9-positive cells relative to uninjected controls was 5.3%) (Figure 7E,E' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: LvAlx4.WT.GFP protein accumulated in the nucleus and was expressed at similar levels as LvAlx1.WT.GFP.
claims.source: We confirmed by fluorescence microscopy that the LvAlx4.WT.GFP protein accumulated in the nucleus and was expressed at similar levels as LvAlx1.WT.GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Replacement of the region between the homeodomain and OAR domain of LvAlx4 with the corresponding region of LvAlx1 resulted in a striking rescue of PMC specification and patterning.
claims.source: Replacement of the region between the homeodomain and OAR domain of LvAlx4 with the corresponding region of LvAlx1 (LvAlx4.LvAlx1C.GFP) resulted in a striking rescue of PMC specification and patterning (mean percentage of 6a9-positive cells relative to uninjected controls was 87%) (Figure 7F,F' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Domain 2 alone is sufficient to confer early skeletogenic function on LvAlx4.
claims.source: The minimum region that was sufficient to confer early skeletogenic function was subsequently narrowed down to Domain 2 (LvAlx4.LvAlx1D2.GFP) (mean percentage of 6a9-positive cells relative to uninjected controls was 96%) (Figure 7G–H' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The chimeric LvAlx4 protein containing LvAlx1 Domain 2 fully rescued later skeletal morphogenesis.
claims.source: We also showed that the chimeric LvAlx4 protein containing LvAlx1 Domain 2 fully rescued later skeletal morphogenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D,K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by DIC microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The gain of Domain 2 might have been a critical innovation that marked the functional specialization of the ancestral alx1 gene.
claims.source: These findings further confirmed the importance of Domain 2 in LvAlx1 function. In addition, they suggested that the gain of this domain might have been a critical innovation that marked the functional specialization of the ancestral alx1 gene.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the experimental findings about Domain 2's importance.

claims.claim: SpAlx1 was interchangeable with LvAlx1.
claims.source: SpAlx1 was interchangeable with LvAlx1 but PmAlx1 was not (Figure 8D–E').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: PmAlx1 was not interchangeable with LvAlx1.
claims.source: SpAlx1 was interchangeable with LvAlx1 but PmAlx1 was not (Figure 8D–E').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: PmAlx1.WT.GFP protein showed nuclear accumulation and robust expression, similar to LvAlx1.WT.GFP.
claims.source: The PmAlx1.WT.GFP protein showed nuclear accumulation and robust expression, similar to LvAlx1.WT.GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: PmAlx1 possesses its own Domain 2.
claims.source: It should also be noted that PmAlx1 possesses its own Domain 2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The protein-level changes in PmAlx1 that limited its function in the sea urchin embryo were located within the C-terminal region between the homeodomain and OAR domain.
claims.source: We found that the protein-level changes in PmAlx1 that limited its function in the sea urchin embryo were located within the C-terminal region between the homeodomain and OAR domain, as a chimeric form of PmAlx1 containing this region of the LvAlx1 protein (PmAlx1.LvAlx1C.GFP) rescued PMC specification and patterning in LvAlx1 morphants (Figure 8F,F').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chimeric protein rescue assays shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Embryos expressing PmAlx1.LvAlx1C.GFP exhibited normal skeletal development at later developmental stages.
claims.source: These embryos also exhibited normal skeletal development at later developmental stages (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E,L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by DIC microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: PmAlx1 Domain 2 is functionally interchangeable with LvAlx1 Domain 2.
claims.source: To determine whether PmAlx1 Domain 2 was functionally interchangeable with LvAlx1 Domain 2, we created an LvAlx1 construct in which the endogenous Domain 2 was replaced by PmAlx1 Domain 2 (LvAlx1.PmAlx1D2.GFP). This chimeric protein efficiently rescued PMC specification and patterning in LvAlx1 morphants (Figure 8G,G'; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The functional conservation of Domain 2 across >450 million years of evolution is striking.
claims.source: These findings highlighted the striking functional conservation of Domain 2 across >450 million years of evolution.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental finding that PmAlx1 Domain 2 is functionally interchangeable with LvAlx1 Domain 2.

claims.claim: The inability of PmAlx1 to support skeletogenesis in sea urchins was attributable to sequence differences within the C-terminal region but outside the conserved Domain 2.
claims.source: At the same time, they showed that the inability of PmAlx1 to support skeletogenesis in sea urchins was attributable to sequence differences within the C-terminal region but outside the conserved Domain 2.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings with chimeric proteins.

claims.claim: The intron-exon organization of the alx4 genes in all echinoderm clades has been strictly conserved.
claims.source: This analysis showed that the intron-exon organization of the alx4 genes in all echinoderm clades has been strictly conserved and corresponds closely to that of the single hemichordate alx4-like gene.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The intron-exon organization of alx4 genes corresponds closely to that of the single hemichordate alx4-like gene.
claims.source: This analysis showed that the intron-exon organization of the alx4 genes in all echinoderm clades has been strictly conserved and corresponds closely to that of the single hemichordate alx4-like gene.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The intron-exon organization of echinoderm alx1 genes is more variable than alx4 genes.
claims.source: By contrast, the intron-exon organization of echinoderm alx1 genes is more variable and in all clades these genes contain greater numbers of exons than their alx4 paralogues.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Echinoderm alx1 genes contain greater numbers of exons than their alx4 paralogues.
claims.source: By contrast, the intron-exon organization of echinoderm alx1 genes is more variable and in all clades these genes contain greater numbers of exons than their alx4 paralogues.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The duplication of the ancestral alx4-like gene was followed by an increase in the structural complexity of the paralogue that was the progenitor of the modern alx1 gene.
claims.source: These findings support the view that the duplication of the ancestral alx4-like gene was followed by an increase in the structural complexity of the paralogue that was the progenitor of the modern alx1 gene.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparative genomic analysis of intron-exon structure.

claims.claim: Nucleotide and protein BLAST searches did not identify Domain 2-like sequences in genes other than alx1.
claims.source: Nucleotide and protein BLAST searches did not identify Domain 2-like sequences in genes other than alx1, either within or outside of the echinoderms, supporting the view that this domain arose de novo within the alx1 gene by the recruitment of non-coding sequences.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis (BLAST searches).

claims.claim: Domain 2 arose de novo within the alx1 gene by the recruitment of non-coding sequences.
claims.source: Nucleotide and protein BLAST searches did not identify Domain 2-like sequences in genes other than alx1, either within or outside of the echinoderms, supporting the view that this domain arose de novo within the alx1 gene by the recruitment of non-coding sequences.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the lack of homologous sequences in other genes.

claims.claim: Intrinsically disordered regions are enriched in domains obtained through exonization of intronic sequences.
claims.source: It has been shown that intrinsically disordered regions are enriched in domains obtained through exonization of intronic sequences (Buljan et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The Domain 3 regions of LvAlx1, SpAlx1, EtAlx1, PpAlx1, PmAlx1 and OsAlx1 are all predicted to be intrinsically disordered.
claims.source: Using InterPro protein sequence analysis and the MobiDB database of intrinsically disordered and mobile proteins, we found that the Domain 3 regions of LvAlx1, SpAlx1, EtAlx1, PpAlx1, PmAlx1 and OsAlx1 are all predicted to be intrinsically disordered, despite their divergent sequences (Finn et al., 2017; Potenza et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis using InterPro and MobiDB.

claims.claim: The intrinsically disordered nature of Domain 3 is consistent with the hypothesis that the Domain (2 + 3) exon arose through the recruitment of previously non-coding sequences.
claims.source: These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that the Domain (2 + 3) exon arose through the recruitment of previously non-coding sequences.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the intrinsic disorder prediction.

claims.claim: Newly born exons are alternatively spliced at a much higher frequency than old exons.
claims.source: Newly born exons are alternatively spliced at a much higher frequency than old exons, and it has been argued that alternative splicing may provide an opportunity for natural selection to act on new protein structures without completely eliminating the parental form (Sorek, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Alternative splicing may provide an opportunity for natural selection to act on new protein structures without completely eliminating the parental form.
claims.source: Newly born exons are alternatively spliced at a much higher frequency than old exons, and it has been argued that alternative splicing may provide an opportunity for natural selection to act on new protein structures without completely eliminating the parental form (Sorek, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature.

claims.claim: In echinozoan alx1 genes, Domains 2 and 3 are contained on a single, separate exon.
claims.source: In echinozoan alx1 genes (Lv-alx1, Sp-alx1, Et-alx1 and Pp-alx1), Domains 2 and 3 are contained on a single, separate exon.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: At all developmental stages tested, the wild-type [i.e. Domain (2 + 3)-containing] Lv-alx1 mRNA was the predominant isoform.
claims.source: We analyzed the pattern of splicing in this region by RT-PCR and found that at all developmental stages tested, the wild-type [i.e. Domain (2 + 3)-containing] Lv-alx1 mRNA was the predominant isoform (Figure 10A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Two minor splice variants of Lv-alx1 were detected.
claims.source: Two minor splice variants were also detected, and these were extracted and sequenced.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: In LvAlx1 splice variant 1, an alternative splice donor site at the 3' end of Domain 3 was utilized, introducing a frameshift and resulting in a premature stop codon within Domain 4.
claims.source: In LvAlx1 splice variant 1, an alternative splice donor site at the 3' end of Domain 3 was utilized, introducing a frameshift and resulting in a premature stop codon within Domain 4.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: In LvAlx1 splice variant 2, the exon containing Domains 2 and 3 was skipped.
claims.source: In LvAlx1 splice variant 2, the exon containing Domains 2 and 3 was skipped.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: RNA-seq data showed one major splicing isoform that contained the Domain (2 + 3) exon and low levels of an isoform lacking this exon.
claims.source: These results closely matched those obtained by RNA-seq, which also showed one major splicing isoform that contained the Domain (2 + 3) exon and low levels of an isoform lacking this exon (Rafiq et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The Domain (2 + 3) exon is alternatively spliced in Eucidaris tribuloides.
claims.source: In addition, in the course of cloning and sequencing alx1 cDNAs from the pencil urchin, Eucidaris tribuloides, we identified a mixture of clones that either contained or lacked the Domain (2 + 3) exon, indicating that this region was also alternatively spliced in this species (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cDNA cloning and sequencing data.

claims.claim: In asterozoans, Domains 2 and 3 of Alx1 are encoded by a continuous open reading frame that also includes a portion of the homeodomain.
claims.source: In contrast to echinozoan alx1 genes, in an asterozoan, Domains 2 and 3 of Alx1 are encoded by a continuous open reading frame that also includes a portion of the homeodomain (Figure 10C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Asterozoan alx1 genes contain a potential splice site at the 5' end of Domain 2 that corresponds perfectly to the 5' splice junction of the echinozoan alx1 genes.
claims.source: We noted that asterozoan alx1 genes contain a potential splice site at the 5' end of Domain 2 that corresponds perfectly to the 5' splice junction of the echinozoan alx1 genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis.

claims.claim: RT-PCR analysis of RNA from P. miniata embryos revealed five major splice variants in the Domain 2 region.
claims.source: RT-PCR analysis of RNA extracted from P. miniata embryos at several developmental stages revealed five major splice variants in this region.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: There is a change in the splicing pattern of PmAlx1 across development, with elevated levels of the wild-type PmAlx1 (which contains the Domain (2 + 3) exon) by the late bipinnaria stage when adult skeletal elements are being produced.
claims.source: We also noted a change in the splicing pattern across development, such that by the late bipinnaria stage, when adult skeletal elements are being produced, levels of the wild-type PmAlx1 which contained the Domain (2 + 3) exon were elevated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data across developmental stages shown in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: The splicing pattern of alx1 in P. miniata is developmentally regulated.
claims.source: These findings revealed a complex pattern of alternative splicing of the alx1 transcript in P. miniata and showed that the splicing pattern is developmentally regulated, with a shift to a greater abundance of the wild-type mRNA isoform (which encodes Domain 2) at stages when skeletogenesis is underway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data across developmental stages shown in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: A short form of Alx1 containing only the homeodomain and Domains 1 and 2 is able to substantially rescue PMC specification and skeletal morphogenesis in sea urchin embryos.
claims.source: Our studies show that a short form of Alx1 containing only the homeodomain and Domains 1 and 2 is able to substantially rescue PMC specification and skeletal morphogenesis in sea urchin (L. variegatus) embryos.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rescue assays shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The OAR domain and N-terminal region of vertebrate Alx1 have modest, attenuating and enhancing influences, respectively, on transcriptional activity.
claims.source: Studies on vertebrate Alx1 have reported that the OAR domain and N-terminal region have modest, attenuating and enhancing influences, respectively, on transcriptional activity (Amendt et al., 1999; Horiguchi and Takeshita, 2003; Norris and Kern, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on vertebrate Alx1.

claims.claim: The OAR domain, N-terminal region, or other domains of Alx1 may play important roles in adult skeletogenesis.
claims.source: It should be noted that our rescue assay specifically examined the embryonic function of Alx1, and the OAR domain, N-terminal region, or other domains of Alx1 may play important roles in adult skeletogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about potential functions not tested in the current study.

claims.claim: Domain 2 may alter DNA binding directly or may act indirectly by recruiting protein partners that influence the transcriptional activity of Alx1.
claims.source: The specific biochemical function of Domain 2 remains to be elucidated. Owning to its proximity to the homeodomain, this domain may alter DNA binding directly or may act indirectly by recruiting protein partners that influence the transcriptional activity of Alx1.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the potential mechanisms by which Domain 2 functions.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of PmAlx1 in S. purpuratus embryos results in ectopic skeletal spicule formation and a radialized skeletal phenotype.
claims.source: Ectopic expression of PmAlx1 in S. purpuratus embryos has been reported to result in ectopic skeletal spicule formation and a radialized skeletal phenotype (McCauley et al., 2012) and we observed the same phenotype in L. variegatus embryos (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and the authors' own observations.

claims.claim: A radialized skeleton can result from a disruption of ectodermal patterning.
claims.source: This result was previously interpreted as evidence of the functional conservation of the PmAlx1 and LvAlx1 proteins, but a radialized skeleton can also result from a disruption of ectodermal patterning (Bergeron et al., 2011; Coffman et al., 2014; Coluccio et al., 2011; Flowers et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on ectodermal patterning.

claims.claim: Functional diversification following gene duplication has been documented in several transcription factor families.
claims.source: Functional diversification following gene duplication has been documented in several transcription factor families, such as the MADS box family in plants, the hox3/zen/bcd family in arthropods, and the myb gene family in vertebrates [reviewed by (Lynch and Wagner, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of previous literature.

claims.claim: The echinoderm alx1 and alx4 genes originated from a gene duplication event.
claims.source: The echinoderm alx1 and alx4 genes, which are physically adjacent to one another, originated from a gene duplication event.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from their physical linkage and sequence similarity.

claims.claim: The alx1/alx4 gene duplication occurred after the divergence of echinoderms from hemichordates and was present in the last common ancestor of all modern echinoderms at least 520 million years ago.
claims.source: Koga et al., 2016 concluded that this duplication occurred after the divergence of echinoderms from hemichordates and was present in the last common ancestor of all modern echinoderms at least 520 million years ago.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: All echinoderms have clear orthologues of alx1 and alx4.
claims.source: This conclusion was based on two observations: (1) all echinoderms have clear orthologues of alx1 and alx4 (also known as calx), and (2) the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii has a single alx4-like gene.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from comparative genomics.

claims.claim: The hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii has a single alx4-like gene.
claims.source: This conclusion was based on two observations: (1) all echinoderms have clear orthologues of alx1 and alx4 (also known as calx), and (2) the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii has a single alx4-like gene.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from genomic data.

claims.claim: The publicly available genome sequences of Ptychodera flava confirm the presence of a single Alx4-like protein that clusters with the S. kowlavskii protein.
claims.source: The publicly available genome sequences of a different hemichordate, Ptychodera flava (http://marinegenomics.oist.jp/) confirms the presence of a single Alx4-like protein that clusters with the S. kowlavskii protein (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Alx1 and Alx4 are not functionally redundant.
claims.source: Our findings clearly show, however, that Alx1 and Alx4 are not functionally interchangeable.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rescue assays shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The lack of rescue by LvAlx4 is not attributable to direct binding of the LvAlx1 MO to LvAlx4.WT.GFP mRNA.
claims.source: The lack of rescue by LvAlx4 is not attributable to direct binding of the LvAlx1 MO to LvAlx4.WT.GFP mRNA, as the N-terminal MO target sequence is not conserved in Lv-alx4.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from sequence comparison of the MO target site.

claims.claim: The gain of Domain 2 was an important evolutionary innovation that marked the functional divergence of Alx1 from Alx4 by conferring skeletogenic capabilities on Alx1.
claims.source: Most strikingly, insertion of the LvAlx1 Domain 2 into LvAlx4 is sufficient to confer function and fully rescue PMC specification, patterning, and skeleton formation in LvAlx1 morphants. This observation strongly supports the view that the gain of Domain 2 was an important evolutionary innovation that marked the functional divergence of Alx1 from Alx4 by conferring skeletogenic capabilities on Alx1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chimeric protein rescue assays shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Protein domains are acquired through several mechanisms, such as gene fusion, intron recombination, exon recombination, retrotransposition and exon extension.
claims.source: Protein domains are acquired through several mechanisms, such as gene fusion, intron recombination, exon recombination, retrotransposition and exon extension (Buljan et al., 2010; Marsh and Teichmann, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on protein domain evolution.

claims.claim: The evolution of the alx1 paralogue was accompanied by an increase in the structural complexity of the gene.
claims.source: By comparing the intron-exon organization of alx1 and alx4 in echinoderms and hemichordates, we have shown that the evolution of the alx1 paralogue was accompanied by an increase in the structural complexity of the gene.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: There is a general tendency for duplicated genes to diverge structurally.
claims.source: This is consistent with a general tendency for duplicated genes to diverge structurally (Xu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on gene duplication.

claims.claim: Domain 2 was originally acquired via recruitment of intronic sequences in an ancestral form of alx1.
claims.source: Based on these considerations, we propose a model whereby Domain 2 was originally acquired via recruitment of intronic sequences in an ancestral form of alx1 (Figure 11).
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on multiple lines of evidence including sequence analysis, intrinsic disorder predictions, and alternative splicing patterns.

claims.claim: Asterozoan alx1 genes have retained the intron-exon structure of the ancestral alx1 gene.
claims.source: We propose that asterozoan alx1 genes have retained the intron-exon structure of the ancestral alx1 gene while echinozoan alx1 genes underwent multiple rounds of intron gain following the exon extension event, including the gain of an intron that separated the Domain 2-containing exon from its parental exon (Figures 9 and 11).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparative genomic analysis.

claims.claim: Echinozoan alx1 genes underwent multiple rounds of intron gain following the exon extension event.
claims.source: We propose that asterozoan alx1 genes have retained the intron-exon structure of the ancestral alx1 gene while echinozoan alx1 genes underwent multiple rounds of intron gain following the exon extension event, including the gain of an intron that separated the Domain 2-containing exon from its parental exon (Figures 9 and 11).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparative genomic analysis.

claims.claim: The intrinsically disordered state of Domain 3 is a vestige of its origin from non-coding sequence.
claims.source: We also propose that the intrinsically disordered state of Domain 3 is a vestige of its origin from non-coding sequence (see Wilson et al., 2017), while the highly conserved Domain 2 has become more ordered over time in concert with its acquisition of an important developmental function.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on intrinsic disorder predictions and evolutionary reasoning.

claims.claim: The highly conserved Domain 2 has become more ordered over time in concert with its acquisition of an important developmental function.
claims.source: We also propose that the intrinsically disordered state of Domain 3 is a vestige of its origin from non-coding sequence (see Wilson et al., 2017), while the highly conserved Domain 2 has become more ordered over time in concert with its acquisition of an important developmental function.

claims.claim: The presence of a well-conserved Domain 2 in the Alx1 protein of sea stars suggests that this domain may have both embryonic and adult functions.
claims.source: The presence of a well-conserved Domain 2 in the Alx1 protein of sea stars, which do not form a larval skeleton, suggests that this domain may have both embryonic and adult functions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of Domain 2 in sea stars despite the absence of larval skeletons.

claims.claim: In sea stars, levels of alx1 mRNA are extremely low in the embryo but increase at larval stages, when alx1 is expressed in the skeletogenic centers of the adult rudiment.
claims.source: It was shown previously that in sea stars, levels of alx1 mRNA are extremely low in the embryo but increase at larval stages, when alx1 is expressed in the skeletogenic centers of the adult rudiment (Koga et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous expression studies.

claims.claim: Regulation of the alternative splicing of alx1 influences the levels of functional (Domain 2-containing) Alx1 protein during development.
claims.source: Our findings indicate that, in addition to this control mechanism, regulation of the alternative splicing of alx1 also influences the levels of functional (Domain 2-containing) Alx1 protein during development.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data showing developmentally regulated splicing patterns in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Adult hemichordates form small, calcareous skeletal elements termed ossicles.
claims.source: In hemichordates, the closest outgroup to echinoderms, the single alx4-like gene lacks Domain 2. Adult hemichordates form small, calcareous skeletal elements termed ossicles, and orthologues of several echinoid biomineralization genes are transcribed during development (Cameron and Bishop, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about hemichordate biology, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The ancestral alx4-like gene may have provided positive inputs into a 'primitive' skeletogenic GRN similar to that present in modern hemichordates.

claims.claim: Gene duplication and the subsequent gain of Domain 2 by Alx1 altered its transcriptional activity, thereby modifying a rudimentary, ancestral skeletogenic GRN in ways that promoted the formation of much more elaborate endoskeletal system.

claims.claim: Exonization of Domain 2 was an early and critically important event in the functional divergence of Alx1 and Alx4 and a major step in the evolution of echinoderm biomineralization.

results.result: A morpholino-resistant rescue assay was successfully established for LvAlx1 structure-function analysis. Six silent mutations were introduced into the MO target site to generate MO-resistant LvAlx1.WT.GFP mRNA, which rescued PMC specification when co-injected with LvAlx1 MO (99% rescue). Controls confirmed that rescue required LvAlx1 protein production and that the assay recapitulated known dose-dependent effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 collectively establish a robust rescue assay system. The experimental design includes appropriate controls (C58: 3STOPS construct showing no rescue, C57: MO alone blocking specification, C59: overexpression inducing supernumerary PMCs), and quantitative data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) demonstrate effective rescue at 99% of control levels. The validation is thorough and well-controlled.

results.result: The putative MAPK phosphorylation site (T28) in LvAlx1 is not required for skeletogenic function. Neither phosphorylation-null (T28A) nor phosphomimetic (T28D) mutations affected the ability of LvAlx1 to rescue morphant embryos (97% and 96% rescue respectively).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by experimental data showing that MAPK site mutations do not affect rescue efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The inference that MAPK signaling in PMC specification is not mediated through Alx1 phosphorylation (C61) is reasonable given the data, though it does not rule out other roles for this site or indirect MAPK effects.

results.result: The N-terminal region of LvAlx1, comprising almost one-third of the protein, is dispensable for skeletogenic function. Deletion of the N-terminal region, charged domain, or all sequences upstream of the homeodomain did not affect rescue of PMC specification and patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are well-supported by systematic deletion analysis (Figure 3). Multiple independent deletions all show full rescue, and the finding is consistent with the low sequence conservation of this region among echinoderms (C66, Figure 1). The conclusion is appropriately limited to the rescue assay context.

results.result: The C-terminal region between the homeodomain and OAR domain contains motifs essential for Alx1 function. While deletion of the highly conserved OAR domain had minimal effect (86% rescue), deletion of the intervening C-terminal region almost completely abolished rescue (1.3% rescue).
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by deletion analysis data (Figure 4). The striking difference between OAR deletion (minimal effect) and C-terminal region deletion (complete loss of function) clearly identifies this region as functionally critical. The quantitative data are robust and the inference (C69) is well-justified.

results.result: Domain 2 is essential for LvAlx1 skeletogenic function while Domains 1, 3, and 4 are dispensable. Systematic deletion analysis revealed that deletion of Domain 2 alone almost completely abolished rescue (7.5%), while deletion of Domains 1, 3, or 4 individually did not affect function (100-101% rescue).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are strongly supported by systematic deletion analysis (Figure 5). The data clearly identify Domain 2 as uniquely essential, with quantitative rescue data for each deletion construct. The experimental design systematically tests each domain, providing strong evidence for the specific importance of Domain 2.

results.result: A minimal construct containing only the homeodomain and Domains 1 and 2 (132 amino acids, less than 1/3 the length of wild-type Alx1) is sufficient for complete rescue of PMC specification, patterning, and skeletogenesis. All mutant proteins showed similar expression levels, nuclear localization, and rescued later skeletal morphogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 are well-supported by experimental data (Figures 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1-2). The minimal construct shows 98% rescue, expression and localization controls are appropriate (C77-C78), NLS analysis confirms nuclear targeting (C79), and later skeletal development is normal (C80). This comprehensively demonstrates sufficiency of the minimal construct.

results.result: LvAlx4 lacks skeletogenic function but insertion of LvAlx1 Domain 2 confers robust skeletogenic function on LvAlx4. LvAlx4 lacks Domain 2 and cannot rescue LvAlx1 morphants (5.3% rescue), but chimeric LvAlx4 containing LvAlx1 Domain 2 fully rescues PMC specification, patterning, and skeleton formation (96% rescue).
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 are strongly supported by experimental data (Figure 7, Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The sequence analysis (C81-C82), functional testing (C83-C84), and chimeric protein experiments (C85-C87) provide compelling evidence that Domain 2 is both necessary and sufficient to confer skeletogenic function. The evolutionary inference (C88) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Alx1 proteins from closely related sea urchin species are functionally interchangeable, but those from distantly related echinoderms are not, despite conservation of Domain 2. SpAlx1 rescued LvAlx1 morphants while PmAlx1 did not, but PmAlx1 Domain 2 is functionally interchangeable with LvAlx1 Domain 2. The functional incompatibility of PmAlx1 is due to sequence differences in the C-terminal region outside Domain 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C97 are well-supported by cross-species expression experiments (Figure 8). The data demonstrate functional interchangeability at close evolutionary distances but not at greater distances, while showing that Domain 2 itself remains functionally conserved across >450 million years. The chimeric protein experiments clearly localize the incompatibility to regions outside Domain 2.

results.result: The intron-exon organization of alx4 genes is strictly conserved across echinoderms and corresponds to the hemichordate alx4-like gene, while alx1 genes show more variable organization with greater numbers of exons. This supports the view that duplication of the ancestral alx4-like gene was followed by increased structural complexity of the alx1 paralogue.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are supported by comparative genomic analysis (Figure 9). The data clearly show conservation of alx4 structure and increased complexity of alx1 genes. The inference about evolutionary trajectory (C102) is reasonable given the comparative data, though alternative scenarios cannot be completely ruled out.

results.result: Domain 2 likely arose de novo within the alx1 gene by recruitment of non-coding sequences (exonization). BLAST searches found no Domain 2-like sequences in other genes, Domain 3 is predicted to be intrinsically disordered (consistent with origin from non-coding sequences), and intrinsically disordered regions are enriched in domains obtained through exonization.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: negative BLAST results (C103), intrinsic disorder predictions (C106), and literature on exonization (C105). However, the conclusion (C104, C107) remains a hypothesis as sequence divergence could obscure homology, and intrinsic disorder is not definitive proof of exonization. The evidence is consistent with but does not prove the exonization hypothesis.

results.result: Domain 2 is subject to alternative splicing in echinozoans. In L. variegatus, the wild-type Domain (2+3)-containing mRNA is the predominant isoform at all developmental stages tested, with two minor splice variants detected. Similar alternative splicing occurs in E. tribuloides.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C116 are supported by RT-PCR and sequencing data (Figure 10A-B). The data clearly show alternative splicing patterns with one predominant isoform and minor variants. The finding in E. tribuloides (C116) provides additional support, though the data are not shown.

results.result: Alternative splicing of alx1 in P. miniata is complex and developmentally regulated. Five major splice variants were detected, with elevated levels of wild-type (Domain 2-containing) PmAlx1 at late bipinnaria stage when adult skeletal elements are being produced.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 are supported by RT-PCR data across developmental stages (Figure 10C-D). The data show multiple splice variants and a clear developmental shift toward the Domain 2-containing isoform during skeletogenesis. This provides strong evidence for developmental regulation of splicing.

results.result: A model is proposed whereby Domain 2 was originally acquired via recruitment of intronic sequences in an ancestral alx1 gene, with asterozoan alx1 genes retaining the ancestral structure while echinozoan alx1 genes underwent multiple rounds of intron gain. The intrinsically disordered Domain 3 is proposed to be a vestige of non-coding origin, while Domain 2 became more ordered over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C144 present an evolutionary model based on comparative genomic data (Figure 9, 11) and intrinsic disorder predictions. While the model is consistent with available evidence, it remains speculative. The claims about ancestral structure retention (C141) and intron gain (C142) are inferences from comparative data. The proposal about Domain 3 disorder (C143) and Domain 2 ordering (C144) are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct evidence of evolutionary trajectories.

results.result: The gain of Domain 2 was an important evolutionary innovation that marked the functional divergence of Alx1 from Alx4 by conferring skeletogenic capabilities on Alx1. Exonization of Domain 2 was an early and critically important event in the functional divergence of Alx1 and Alx4 and a major step in the evolution of echinoderm biomineralization.
results.evaluation: Claims C136 and C152 represent the major evolutionary conclusion of the study. These are strongly supported by the combined experimental evidence showing: (1) Domain 2 is essential for Alx1 function, (2) Alx4 lacks Domain 2 and skeletogenic function, (3) insertion of Domain 2 confers function on Alx4, (4) Domain 2 is highly conserved across echinoderms, and (5) evidence for exonization. While the evolutionary narrative involves inference, it is well-supported by the experimental data.

results.result: Other protein-level changes in Alx1 have accumulated more recently and limit the functional interchangeability of Alx1 proteins among echinoderms.
results.evaluation: Claim C153 is supported by cross-species expression experiments (Figure 8) showing that PmAlx1 cannot rescue LvAlx1 morphants due to sequence differences outside Domain 2. This demonstrates that additional protein-level changes beyond Domain 2 have accumulated and affect function, though the specific changes and their timing remain to be determined.

results.result: A novel, conserved motif (Domain 2) essential for skeletogenic function was identified through structure-function analysis. Domain 2 is highly conserved across echinoderms, subject to alternative splicing, and evidence suggests it was gained through exonization. A gene duplication event permitted functional specialization of Alx1 through changes in exon-intron organization, supporting the evolution of a major morphological novelty.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C4, C6-C9 represent the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental and comparative analyses presented throughout the manuscript. The identification of Domain 2 (C2), its functional importance (C4), conservation (C6), alternative splicing (C7), and evidence for exonization (C8) are all supported by data. The evolutionary conclusion (C9) integrates these findings into a coherent narrative about transcription factor evolution and morphological novelty.
